questions.question: Describe the structure of fullerenes and give one use.
questions.modelAnswer: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow cages or tubes. One use is drug delivery, lubricants or reinforcing materials.
markingPoints: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow cages or tubes. One use is drug delivery, lubricants or reinforcing materials.

questions.question: Describe the structure of carbon nanotubes and give one use.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon nanotubes are long hollow cylinders of carbon atoms. They have a high length-to-diameter ratio and can conduct electricity. They are used in electronics or as reinforcing materials.
markingPoints: Carbon nanotubes are long hollow cylinders of carbon atoms. They have a high length-to-diameter ratio and can conduct electricity. They are used in electronics or as reinforcing materials.

questions.question: Hydrogen chloride is covalent, but hydrochloric acid solution conducts electricity. Explain both statements.
questions.modelAnswer:
In hydrogen chloride molecules, hydrogen and chlorine share electrons, so the bonding is covalent.
Pure hydrogen chloride consists of neutral molecules and does not conduct.
When dissolved in water, it forms mobile H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
These ions carry charge through the solution.
markingPoints: In hydrogen chloride molecules, hydrogen and chlorine share electrons, so the bonding is covalent.
Pure hydrogen chloride consists of neutral molecules and does not conduct.
When dissolved in water, it forms mobile H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
These ions carry charge through the solution.

questions.question: Classify magnesium oxide as ionic or covalent. Explain your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium oxide is ionic. Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions.
markingPoints: Magnesium oxide is ionic. Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions.

questions.question: Classify carbon dioxide as ionic or covalent. Explain your answer.

questions.question: Explain fully how magnesium and chlorine form magnesium chloride, MgCl₂. Include electron transfer, ion charges and electrostatic attraction.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.
Each of two chlorine atoms (2,8,7) gains one electron to form two Cl⁻ ions.
Oppositely charged ions attract strongly in all directions by electrostatic forces, forming a giant ionic lattice.
Chemical formula MgCl₂ balances charge.
markingPoints: Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.
Each of two chlorine atoms (2,8,7) gains one electron to form two Cl⁻ ions.
Oppositely charged ions attract strongly in all directions by electrostatic forces, forming a giant ionic lattice.
Chemical formula MgCl₂ balances charge.

questions.question: Explain why a wire made from a pure metal usually conducts electricity better than a wire made from an alloy.
questions.modelAnswer: Both contain delocalised electrons that carry charge. In an alloy, different-sized atoms distort the regular layers. This makes it harder for the delocalised electrons to move through the structure, so the alloy has lower electrical conductivity.
markingPoints: Both contain delocalised electrons that carry charge. In an alloy, different-sized atoms distort the regular layers. This makes it harder for the delocalised electrons to move through the structure, so the alloy has lower electrical conductivity.

questions.question: Aluminium conducts electricity better than sodium. Explain this using metallic bonding.
questions.modelAnswer: Both metals have delocalised electrons. Each aluminium atom provides three delocalised electrons, whereas each sodium atom provides one. More delocalised electrons are available to carry charge in aluminium.
markingPoints: Both metals have delocalised electrons. Each aluminium atom provides three delocalised electrons, whereas each sodium atom provides one. More delocalised electrons are available to carry charge in aluminium.

questions.question: A substance has a melting point of −15 °C and a boiling point of 75 °C. State whether it is solid, liquid or gas at −20 °C, 25 °C and 90 °C. Explain your answers.
questions.modelAnswer:
At −20 °C it is a solid because the temperature is below its melting point.
At 25 °C it is a liquid because the temperature is above its melting point but below its boiling point.
At 90 °C it is a gas because the temperature is above its boiling point.
markingPoints: At −20 °C it is a solid because the temperature is below its melting point.
At 25 °C it is a liquid because the temperature is above its melting point but below its boiling point.

questions.modelAnswer: Solid, liquid and gas.
markingPoints: Solid, liquid and gas.

questions.question: Describe the structure of solids in terms of particles?
questions.modelAnswer: Particles are close together in fixed positions and form a regular structure. There are strong forces of attraction between the particles. The particles vibrate in position.
markingPoints: Particles are close together in fixed positions and form a regular structure. There are strong forces of attraction between the particles. The particles vibrate in position.

questions.question: Describe the structure of liquids in terms of particles?

markingPoints: Particles are close together but can move over each other. There are weak forces of attraction between the particles. The particles are constantly moving.

questions.question: Describe the structure of gases in terms of particles?

markingPoints: Particles are far apart. There are very weak forces of attraction between the particles. Particles move constantly in straight lines.

questions.question: Three metals could be used for overhead power cables. Aluminium: conductivity 38 units, density 2.7 g/cm³, £1.50/kg. Copper: 60 units, 9.0 g/cm³, £7.00/kg. Silver: 63 units, 10.5 g/cm³, £640/kg. Choose the most suitable metal and justify your choice using the data.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium is the best overall choice for overhead cables. It conducts less well than copper and silver, but is much lighter and far cheaper. questions.question: Explain why an ionic solid is brittle when struck, whereas a pure metal can be bent into shape.

In a pure metal, layers of atoms can slide past each other while metallic bonding is maintained by delocalised electrons, so the metal can bend.

Like charges repel, so the lattice splits.
In a pure metal, layers of atoms can slide past each other while metallic bonding is maintained by delocalised electrons, so the metal can bend.

questions.question: Define a monomer and a polymer.
questions.modelAnswer: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to other molecules. A polymer is a large molecule made from many repeating monomer units.
markingPoints: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to other molecules. A polymer is a large molecule made from many repeating monomer units.

questions.question: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Explain using bonding and structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each graphite carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move and carry charge.
Each diamond carbon bonds to four others, so all outer electrons are localised in covalent bonds.
markingPoints: Each graphite carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move and carry charge.
Each diamond carbon bonds to four others, so all outer electrons are localised in covalent bonds.

questions.question: Explain why giant covalent structures have high melting points.
questions.modelAnswer: Many strong covalent bonds need to be broken.
markingPoints: Many strong covalent bonds need to be broken.

questions.question: Explain why most giant covalent structures do not conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: They have no mobile ions or delocalised electrons.
markingPoints: They have no mobile ions or delocalised electrons.

questions.question: A sample has a high melting point and does not conduct electricity as a solid or when molten. Identify the likely structure and give a reason for each property.
questions.modelAnswer:
It is likely a giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, giving a high melting point.
There are no mobile ions or delocalised electrons to carry electrical charge, so it does not conduct in either state.
markingPoints: It is likely a giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, giving a high melting point.
There are no mobile ions or delocalised electrons to carry electrical charge, so it does not conduct in either state.

questions.question: Describe the general structure of giant covalent structures?
questions.modelAnswer: The atoms are in the structures are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds.
markingPoints: The atoms are in the structures are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds.

questions.question: Describe the properties of giant covalent structures?
questions.modelAnswer: They are solids with high melting points.
markingPoints: They are solids with high melting points.

questions.question: Give three examples of giant covalent structures?

questions.question: Name the following giant covalent structures?

questions.question:
Substance A has mp 801 °C and conducts only when molten.
B has mp −98 °C and never conducts.
C has mp 3550 °C and conducts as a solid; it is soft.
D has mp 1710 °C and never conducts.
Part (a): Identify the most likely structure type of each.
Part (b): Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
A giant ionic: high mp.
Mobile ions only molten.
B simple molecular: low mp.
No mobile charge.
C graphite/giant covalent layered carbon: very high mp, delocalised electrons, soft layers.
D giant covalent such as SiO₂: very high mp and no mobile charge.
markingPoints: A giant ionic: high mp.
Mobile ions only molten.
B simple molecular: low mp.
No mobile charge.
C graphite/giant covalent layered carbon: very high mp, delocalised electrons, soft layers.
D giant covalent such as SiO₂: very high mp and no mobile charge.

questions.question: What is an alloy?
questions.modelAnswer: An alloy is a mixture of metals e.g. 18 carat Gold is a mixture of gold and silver.
markingPoints: An alloy is a mixture of metals e.g. 18 carat Gold is a mixture of gold and silver.

questions.question: Describe the general structure of metals and alloys?
questions.modelAnswer: Giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding.

questions.question: What are the general properties of metals?

questions.question: How are the atoms arranged in pure metals?
questions.modelAnswer: Atoms in metals are arranged in layers. These layers can slide over each other.

questions.question: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals?

questions.question: Why are metals good conductors of thermal energy?

questions.modelAnswer:

Giant covalent structures have very high melting points.
Graphite conducts, so several properties are needed rather than one result.

questions.question: Explain why testing only one physical property may be insufficient to identify an unknown bonding type.
questions.modelAnswer:
Different structures can share a property and exceptions exist, such as graphite conducting.
A conclusion based on several independent properties is better supported.

questions.question: Compare the structures and electrical conductivity of diamond and graphite.
questions.modelAnswer: Both are giant covalent structures. In diamond, each carbon forms four bonds and there are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon forms three bonds and one electron per carbon is delocalised, so it conducts.
markingPoints: Both are giant covalent structures. In diamond, each carbon forms four bonds and there are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon forms three bonds and one electron per carbon is delocalised, so it conducts.

questions.question: Give one use of graphite that follows from its properties.

questions.question: Compare the properties of thermosetting and thermosoftening polymers in terms of their structures.

Thermosets have strong cross-links between chains, preventing sliding, so they do not soften readily.

questions.question: A cube-shaped nanoparticle has side length 5.0 nm. Calculate its surface area, volume and simplest surface area : volume ratio.
questions.modelAnswer:
Surface area = 6 × 5.0² = 150 nm².
Volume = 5.0³ = 125 nm³.
Surface area : volume = 150 : 125 = 6 : 5.
markingPoints: Surface area = 6 × 5.0² = 150 nm².
Volume = 5.0³ = 125 nm³.
Surface area : volume = 150 : 125 = 6 : 5.

questions.question: A nanoparticle cube has side 10 nm and a larger cube has side 1 μm. Explain why the nanoparticle has a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
questions.modelAnswer:
Surface area scales with length squared while volume scales with length cubed.
As size decreases, volume falls faster than surface area, so surface area per unit volume increases.
markingPoints: Surface area scales with length squared while volume scales with length cubed.
As size decreases, volume falls faster than surface area, so surface area per unit volume increases.

questions.question: Explain why pure metals are usually more malleable than alloys and why alloys are often harder.
questions.modelAnswer:
In a pure metal, equal-sized atoms form regular layers that slide.
An alloy contains different-sized atoms that distort the layers and obstruct their movement, so more force is needed and the alloy is harder.
markingPoints: In a pure metal, equal-sized atoms form regular layers that slide.
An alloy contains different-sized atoms that distort the layers and obstruct their movement, so more force is needed and the alloy is harder.

questions.question: Explain why nanoparticles can be more effective catalysts than the same mass of larger particles and why only a small mass may be needed.
questions.modelAnswer:
Smaller particles have a much larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
For the same mass, more atoms are exposed at the surface, providing more active sites and increasing collision frequency/rate.
Therefore a smaller mass can give the required effect.
markingPoints: Smaller particles have a much larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
